newsitem.title: USA: Boeing 737s may get rudder limiters - report.
newsitem.headline: Boeing 737s may get rudder limiters - report.

text.p: Boeing Co. may ask airlines to install new safety devices to limit possible unwanted rudder movement in its widely used 737 jets, the Seattle Times reported Sunday.

Boeing officials confirmed that the company has discussed the possibility of retrofitting the jets with rudder limiting devices after a series of incidents over the past six years, including two unexplained crashes, but they said no decisions had been made.

"We are looking at the possibility," Boeing spokesman Russ Young said. "There haven't been any decisions at this point about whether we're going to do one, what the design would be or whether it would be necessary."
The Seattle newspaper, quoting an unidentified person who has been involved in the discussions, said a decision to install the devices has been made and will be announced soon.

The 737 is the world's most widely used jet, with more than 2,700 in service, and it has a better-than-average safety record. But concerns about uncommanded rudder "hardovers" have grown, especially since a USAir jet crashed into a ravine in 1994 on approach to Pittsburgh, killing all 132 aboard.
That accident is still under investigation, and federal safety officials have been unable to find the cause of a similar 1991 crash in Colorado Springs, Colo., that killed 25.

On Friday the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration ordered that all 737s be tested for rudder safety problems within 10 days and then about once a month after a new series of tests conducted by Boeing found that certain conditions within the power control unit could lead to a "hardover," or uncommanded rudder reversal.
Young said Boeing engineers were working on a way to fix the power control unit flaw.
National Transportation Safety Board Chairman Jim Hall said in a statement that the agency is studying the latest tests for clues to the Colorado Springs and Pittsburgh accidents.
The NTSB investigations already have led the agency to recommend a series of safety improvements to the 737 fleet, including changes that would prevent uncommanded rudder movements.
